t: Before they met Europeans the Guarani called themselves Abá, “men” or “people”; the name Guarani was first applied by Jesuit missionaries to those who had accepted Christianity.
Paulista slave raiders destroyed most of the early Jesuit missions, and within two years 60,000 converts were carried off for sale to São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.
The Guarani language is an official language of Paraguay and Bolivia, and as of 2012 an estimated 90% of the people in Paraguay spoke it.
dyk: When an 800-strong Paulista army attacked the missions in 1641, it was met on the Acaray River by Christian Guarani armed with guns, and its defeat in two battles warded off invasions for ten years.
ev: Aracare, a chief from the Jejuy River, was hanged by the Spanish, prompting an unsuccessful rebellion by Tabare
Loreto, the first Jesuit mission of Guayrá, was founded on the Paranapanema
Paulistas burned the San Antonio mission, killed many and carried the rest into slavery
A Guarani army armed with guns defeated the Paulistas in two battles on the Acaray River
The 30 Guarani missions held 141,252 converts, guarded by an army of 7,000 Guaranis
The Guarani fought for their land against the Treaty of Madrid in the Guarani War
The Jesuits were expelled from Spanish dominions, and the missions soon declined
The Chiriguanos led by Apiaguaiki Tumpa were defeated in the Battle of Kuruyuki

f.homeland: Traditionally the land between the Paraná River and the lower Paraguay River in what is now Paraguay, the Misiones Province of Argentina, southern Brazil once as far east as Rio de Janeiro, and parts of Uruguay and Bolivia; today mainly Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay, with the Eastern Bolivian Guarani in the Gran Chaco near the Pilcomayo River
f.period: First encountered by Europeans in the early 16th century; the Jesuit missions from 1610 until the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767; the Guarani War of 1754–1756; the Bolivian Chiriguanos resisting until the Battle of Kuruyuki in 1892; a living people today
f.known: the Guarani language, an official language of Paraguay and Bolivia; communal houses (malocas); the Jesuit missions, which held more than 100,000 people; the mission army that defeated the Paulista slave raiders in 1641; the Guarani War against the Treaty of Madrid; myths of Ñamandu, Tupã and the Pombero
f.sources: Spanish and Jesuit records, among them Antonio Ruiz de Montoya’s The Spiritual Conquest and the accounts of Martin Dobrizhoffer; letters such as Francisco González de Paniagua’s of 1545 and the caciques of San Luis’s of 1768; mission censuses; myths compiled by the Universidad Nacional de Misiones; modern historians such as Barbara Ganson
